strengths: The core idea is novel and well-motivated: using GHNs with a CNN decoder as both a data generator and a weight-space alignment mechanism, and then patch-tokenizing the resulting weights so that a DiT can generate networks whose width is decoupled from the tokenization scheme. This combination of ideas (graph-conditioned alignment + flexible patch-based diffusion) appears genuinely new in the weight-generation literature.

The paper provides empirical support for its key premise: Figure 3, Figure 4, and Table 1 show that GHN-generated weights exhibit consistent, spatially correlated structure across seeds whereas SGD-trained weights do not, and the nearest-neighbor diversity analysis (Table 1, Table 6, Figure 5) reasonably rules out mode collapse as the explanation.

The central experimental result is convincing within its scope: Table 2 shows NNiT maintaining 86-100% success on held-out topologies while D2NWG degrades sharply (59%, 42%) and SANE fails entirely, and Table 3/Table 4 demonstrate joint architecture-weight synthesis with high success rates. Deploying generated policies directly in ManiSkill3 is a stringent test compared to likelihood or reconstruction metrics.

The method is technically coherent: the MoNL-based dual-timestep training cleanly supports both joint generation p(a,w) and conditional synthesis p(w|a) in one model, and the padding/cropping deployment procedure is clearly described. The limitations section is honest about the MLP-only, four-hidden-layer scope and the training difficulty of deeper models.

The appendix provides substantial reproducibility detail: dataset construction pipeline, filtering thresholds, GHN training hyperparameters, and diffusion training configurations (Tables 5 and 7), plus qualitative rollouts across many architectures (Figures 7-9).
weaknesses: The 'width-agnostic' and 'zero-shot generalization' claims are overreached relative to the evidence. The width vocabulary is only {16, 32, 64}, depth is fixed at 4 hidden layers, and the 'unseen' test topologies are merely new orderings of widths already seen in training (e.g., [32,32,16,64]). There is no evaluation on truly out-of-distribution widths (e.g., 48, 128, 256) or depths, so it remains untested whether the patch tokenization actually transfers to genuinely new geometries rather than recombining familiar patches.

The generated networks are bounded by the GHN-induced training distribution: NNiT learns to sample GHN outputs, not the full distribution of SGD-trained networks. The paper does not test whether NNiT can generate or transfer to SGD-trained weights, so the practical value of the generator beyond the GHN's own weight-quality ceiling is unclear. The framing of this as general 'neural network generation' is stronger than what is demonstrated.

The theoretical claim that GHNs with CNN decoders 'structurally align the weight space' is supported only by qualitative heatmaps (banding patterns) and coarse diversity statistics. There is no quantitative alignment metric, no ablation isolating the CNN decoder (vs. MLP decoder or GHN architecture choices), and no analysis of whether the banding is a meaningful functional structure or an artifact of the shared decoder/normalization. Section 4 would benefit from an ablation on the alignment mechanism.

Baseline comparisons are thin and possibly unfair. SANE fails even on seen architectures (1-6% success), which suggests a misconfigured or poorly adapted baseline rather than an inherent deficiency; there are only two baselines, both adapted by the authors, and no comparison against a straightforward alternative such as training the DiT on canonicalized SGD weights (e.g., Git re-Basin alignment) to test whether GHN alignment is actually necessary.

The evaluation protocol (top-10 of 100 generated samples, 50 episodes each) implies a substantial offline validation cost per deployment, which partially undercuts the 'no retraining, instant deployment' motivation; the paper does not report compute cost of this selection phase, number of evaluation seeds, or statistical significance of the gaps between methods.

Writing quality issues reduce clarity: typos and encoding artifacts ('Sch”urholt'), circular phrasing ('leverage the structural alignment of the structurally aligned weight spaces'), and some unsupported extrapolations in the discussion (e.g., framing depth as a temporal dimension and suggesting a path to 'billion-parameter foundation models' that is not grounded in the experiments).

No code release or artifact availability is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the multi-stage pipeline (128 GHN ensemble training, policy distillation, filtering, diffusion training) despite the detailed hyperparameter tables.

strengths: The core idea is appealing: treating aligned weight matrices as locally structured fields and tokenizing them into patches is a clean way to decouple weight generation from fixed matrix dimensions, and the analogy to variable-resolution image generation is well motivated.

Jointly modeling discrete architecture tokens and continuous weight patches in a single multimodal diffusion transformer (via MoNL-style dual timesteps) is a sensible and non-trivial engineering contribution that enables both p(w|a) and p(a,w) in one model.
The paper is upfront about its pipeline: the dataset of 6,400 GHN-distilled policies, filtering criteria, and hyperparameters are documented in the appendix, and a limitations section is included.
The alignment-vs-mode-collapse checks (nearest-neighbor L2/cosine metrics in Tables 1 and 6, Figure 6) are a thoughtful attempt to show the GHN-induced structure does not collapse diversity.
The zero-shot conditional generation results (Table 2) show a clear separation from D2NWG on unseen topologies, which supports the patch-tokenization hypothesis within the tested setting.
weaknesses: A critical missing baseline: the authors themselves show the GHN generator achieves ~99% success (Table 1). Since GHNs are explicitly designed to predict parameters for unseen architectures (Knyazev et al., 2021), the paper must demonstrate that NNiT outperforms the GHN teacher on unseen topologies, or otherwise articulate what the diffusion model adds. No such comparison is provided, so the entire pipeline may be a roundabout way of reproducing GHN outputs, undermining the paper's central value proposition.

The setup is circular: NNiT is trained exclusively on GHN-generated weights, so the 'structurally aligned weight space' being learned is a property of the GHN artifact distribution, not of natural (SGD-trained) weight spaces. The claimed practical benefit of bypassing training is also weakened, since constructing the corpus required training 128 GHNs plus RL-based filtering of 72 architectures.

The 'zero-shot width generalization' claim is overstated. Held-out architectures are only recombinations of widths already seen during training (16, 32, 64) at fixed depth 4. No extrapolation to genuinely new widths (beyond the padded grid M) or depths is tested, and no ablation isolates whether the padding/cropping scheme rather than the diffusion model is doing the work.

The structural alignment claim rests largely on visual inspection of magnitude heatmaps (Figures 3-4). The only quantitative evidence (diversity metrics) does not directly measure alignment, and the authors concede the input layer shows banding for SGD too. A quantitative alignment metric (e.g., cross-seed correlation after permutation matching) is needed.

Baseline treatment is questionable: SANE fails catastrophically (1% success even on seen architectures) after the authors' own adaptation, and the explanation via positional-embedding index shifts suggests possible mis-configuration rather than a fundamental limitation. A single adapted run per baseline, without tuning effort parity, weakens the comparative claims.

Evaluation uses the top-10 of 100 generated samples with an offline validation phase, which substantially inflates reported success rates; mean-of-samples performance is not reported in the main results, and there is no reporting of seed variance for NNiT training runs.

Several methodological details needed for reproducibility are missing: patch size p, the maximal grid width M, model size/depth of the DiT, number of sampling steps at inference, and no code release is mentioned.

Presentation quality is uneven: typos and grammatical errors ('the structurally weight-space induced by the GHN', 'Sch"urholt' rendering, stray capitalization), a vague L_vb definition, and speculative future-work claims (synthesizing billion-parameter foundation models) that are unsupported by any experiment.

Significance is limited: the method applies only to small MLP policies on three simple ManiSkill tasks with a tiny width vocabulary, one of which (StackCubeEasy) is a custom, simplified variant. The gap between this scope and the framing (general width-agnostic neural network generation) is large.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and well-motivated problem in neural parameter generation: generative priors are typically coupled to fixed matrix dimensions, preventing width-agnostic synthesis. The patch-based tokenization of weight matrices is a clean, sensible mechanism for decoupling the tokenization scheme from layer width, analogous to variable-resolution image generation.

The insight that GHNs with a CNN decoder produce a structurally aligned (spatially correlated) weight distribution—making patch-based modeling feasible in the first place—is novel and empirically supported by Figure 3 heatmaps and the diversity analysis in Tables 1 and 6 showing that alignment does not come from mode collapse.

The multimodal MoNL framework combining discrete architecture tokens and continuous weight patches is well-executed and enables a capability (joint p(a,w) generation) that the baselines cannot support at all (Table 3).

The experimental protocol is reasonably thorough: 64 training and 8 held-out topologies, three ManiSkill3 environments, expert-policy baselines, and detailed hyperparameter and dataset-generation appendices (Tables 5 and 7) that aid reproducibility. The limitation that experiments cover only shallow MLPs is honestly disclosed.

Zero-shot transfer results (Table 2) show a large and consistent gap in the hypothesized direction: NNiT maintains 86-99% success on unseen topologies while D2NWG drops to 42-89% and SANE fails outright, with a plausible mechanistic explanation for SANE's failure (global positional index shift under varying widths).
weaknesses: A critical baseline is missing: sampling weights directly from the GHN ensemble that produced the training data. Since the entire training corpus consists of GHN-generated weights (Section A), and GHNs already generate weights for arbitrary (including unseen) architectures, the paper does not establish that NNiT adds value over the very mechanism that created its training distribution. Without this comparison, the central claim that NNiT is a useful width-agnostic generator is not fully supported.

The core object being modeled is a distribution over GHN outputs, not over genuinely trained networks. This creates a circularity concern: the paper's structural alignment result (Section 4, Figure 3) partly reflects the GHN's deterministic shared decoder rather than a property of neural weight spaces in general, limiting the generality and significance of the contribution. The paper does not test patch tokenization on SGD-trained weight populations or explain why alignment over GHN outputs transfers to real-world use.

Scope is narrow: only MLPs with 4 hidden layers, widths from a 3-element vocabulary {16, 32, 64}, and three closely related cube-manipulation tasks. All 'unseen' topologies are shallow permutations of seen width values, so generalization claims are modest extrapolations rather than demonstrations of width-agnostic synthesis at scale. Speculative statements about extending to billion-parameter foundation models are unsupported.

Evaluation protocol is generous: reporting top-10 of 100 generated samples simulates an offline selection phase that inflates apparent quality, and results are averaged over few repetitions with unclear seed variance for the unseen-architecture condition (Tables 2-4 report single runs in Table 4). The gap between NNiT and the dataset is also nontrivial for StackCubeEasy (86% vs 94%).

The structural alignment evidence is primarily qualitative (visual banding in Figures 3-4); no quantitative measure of local spatial correlation or cross-seed alignment is provided, and Figure 3 shows that the first layer exhibits banding under SGD as well, so the claimed distinction is confined to later layers.

Baselines were retrained/adapted by the authors on the GHN-aligned dataset; SANE's complete failure (0-6% even on seen architectures) suggests possible misconfiguration rather than a fair comparison, and the paper's attribution of this failure to positional-embedding index shift is asserted without direct verification.
No code or data release is mentioned, which, combined with the multi-stage pipeline (128 GHNs, distillation expert, diffusion training), makes independent reproduction difficult.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: prior weight-generation methods are coupled to fixed matrix widths, and patch-based tokenization over a structurally aligned weight space is a sensible route to width-agnostic generation. The framing of weights as spatially correlated fields, analogous to image/video diffusion, is original in this context.

The empirical validation of the central premise (GHNs induce structural alignment) is unusually thorough: cross-seed heatmap visualizations (Fig. 3, 5), nearest-neighbor diversity metrics (Tables 1, 5), CKA analysis (Table 6) ruling out mode collapse, and a controlled permutation ablation (Appendix C.2) showing zero-shot performance collapses from 78.8% to 0% when alignment is destroyed. This directly supports the paper's key claim.

The evaluation is more careful than typical papers in this area: Table 9 reports the full 80-policy distribution (not just top-10), showing the gap over D2NWG is distributional rather than a selection artifact, and the 'worst architecture' comparison is a convincing robustness check.

The pipeline transfers beyond the main setting (MNIST at 96.1% mean accuracy on held-out architectures), and joint architecture+weight synthesis with diversity analysis (Appendix I) is a genuinely novel capability in weight-space generative modeling.
Honest limitations section, detailed reproducibility information (dataset generation, filtering criteria, full hyperparameters in Appendices D-E), and good presentation throughout.
weaknesses: A fundamental scoping issue is under-addressed: the model can only generate weights within the GHN-induced distribution, not SGD-trained networks. Since GHNs are already width-agnostic generators by design, the paper does not convincingly justify why the diffusion transformer on top is necessary—what does NNiT provide beyond direct sampling from the GHN ensemble? Table 1 shows the GHN itself achieves ~99% success on the same architecture, comparable to NNiT's results. The added value (learned joint distribution over architectures, diversity) is asserted but not benchmarked against GHN sampling directly.

The experimental scope is narrow: only 4-hidden-layer MLPs, widths from {16, 32, 64}, a tiny 72-architecture search space, and three ManiSkill tasks (one of which, StackCubeEasy-v1, is custom-designed to be easier). 'Unseen architectures' therefore means interpolating among a very small discrete width vocabulary; generalization to genuinely different width regimes or deeper networks remains untested.

Generated policies are only usable after a top-10 selection from 100 samples; the mean success over all generated policies is 54.9%–78.8% (Table 9), meaning a substantial fraction of samples are not deployable. The practical reliability of the generator is weaker than the headline '>85%' figure suggests.

Claims about 'resolving permutation symmetry' are somewhat overstated: the GHN sidesteps rather than resolves the symmetry, and this only works because the entire training corpus comes from one generator family. The approach does not apply to the practically important setting of generating models trained by SGD, which limits the broader significance of the contribution.

No code release is mentioned, and given the complex multi-stage pipeline (128 GHNs, distillation corpus, diffusion training), reproducibility is a concern. The SANE baseline failure analysis, while plausible, is post-hoc; additional baselines (e.g., a patch-based ablation without GHN alignment, or FiT-style variable resolution on unaligned weights) would strengthen the attribution of gains to the proposed components.

strengths: The core observation — that GHNs with a CNN decoder induce a spatially aligned, permutation-resolved weight distribution that permits patch-based (image-like) generative modeling — is interesting and clearly articulated, and Figure 3 plus the CKA analysis (Table 6) provide convincing visual and quantitative evidence for it.

The permutation ablation (Appendix C.2) is a well-designed control: destroying alignment via random neuron permutations while preserving all per-layer statistics collapses zero-shot performance from 78.8% to 0%, directly establishing that NNiT depends on structural alignment rather than weight statistics.

The paper is transparent about its headline metric: Appendix F reports the full 80-policy distribution (mean 78.8%/74.7%/54.9% success), so the top-10 selection effect is quantified rather than hidden, and the worst-architecture comparison (Table 9) strengthens the claim over D2NWG.

The experimental protocol is reasonably detailed and reproducible on paper: dataset construction (Table 7), diffusion hyperparameters (Table 8), filtering thresholds, held-out architecture splits, and diversity analyses are all specified, and the limitations section honestly identifies the MLP-only, ≤4-hidden-layer scope.

Joint modeling of discrete architecture tokens and continuous weight patches via MoNL (Appendix A) is a clean formulation, and the MNIST transfer (Appendix H) shows the pipeline is not purely task-specific.
weaknesses: A critical missing baseline: the training corpus is entirely GHN-generated, and Table 1 shows the GHN itself already achieves ~99% success on the very architectures in question. Since GHNs are by construction capable of predicting weights for unseen architectures (Knyazev et al., 2021), the paper never establishes what NNiT adds over directly querying the GHN generator — the one comparison that would justify the added complexity is absent. The claimed benefit (sampling diversity, joint p(a,w)) is not demonstrated to be worth the pipeline given a 3^4 = 81-configuration search space.

The contribution is confined to a self-generated synthetic distribution: NNiT demonstrably fails on permuted (functionally identical, SGD-like) weights, so it cannot generate, align with, or transfer to real SGD-trained networks. This severely limits practical significance — the model generates 'GHN-flavored' weights, not learned network parameters, and the paper's framing as general 'width-agnostic neural network generation' overstates this.

The generalization claim is weak in absolute terms: 'zero-shot' transfer is evaluated over 8 held-out topologies drawn from a tiny discrete vocabulary ({16, 32, 64} widths, fixed depth 4, 64 training configurations). Interpolating over a 3×3×3×3 grid is a modest test of width-agnosticism; extrapolation beyond the training vocabulary or depth is never attempted.

Headline numbers rely on the top-10-of-100 selection protocol; while Appendix F is commendably transparent, the abstract's '>85% success on unseen topologies' is not what the unconditional generation achieves (mean 54.9% on StackCubeEasy-v1), which risks misleading readers.

Baseline adaptation appears fragile: SANE fails even on seen architectures (1% success), which the authors attribute to positional-embedding issues under mixed widths; this suggests the baselines may be under-tuned for the setting rather than fundamentally incapable, weakening the comparative evidence.

The structural-alignment argument is largely empirical/visual (banding patterns, cross-seed correlation r ≈ 0.65); there is no theoretical or mechanistic account of why the CNN decoder induces this alignment, or of when it would and would not hold for other architectures/tasks.

Scale is small throughout: three simple ManiSkill manipulation tasks (one custom-eased variant), MLP-only policies, batch size 16, and a 6,400-sample corpus. The generality claims in the limitations and future work (billion-parameter foundation models, linear attention) are speculative relative to what is shown.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies two genuine obstacles in neural weight generation (coupling of generative priors to fixed matrix dimensions, and permutation symmetry) and addresses both with a coherent design.

The idea of using a GHN with a CNN decoder as a mechanism to induce structurally aligned, spatially correlated weight fields is a novel and interesting reframing of GHNs, previously used only as predictors, into a data-generation/alignment tool for generative modeling.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: a permutation ablation (Appendix C.2) cleanly shows zero-shot performance collapsing from 78.8% to 0% when alignment is destroyed, which directly supports the central hypothesis; CKA and nearest-neighbor diversity analyses (Appendices B, C, G) address the plausible confound of mode collapse; Table 9 reports full 80-policy distributions to show the top-10 protocol is not creating the reported gap.

The paper demonstrates a capability that baselines lack—zero-shot conditional weight synthesis for unseen widths (Table 2: 86–100% vs. D2NWG's 42–89%)—and additionally shows joint architecture-weight generation, which no baseline supports (Table 3, Appendix I).

Presentation is generally clear, with good figures (Fig. 2 framework overview, Fig. 3 alignment visualization) and an honest limitations section discussing depth/width constraints and training instability of continuous unbounded weights.
Cross-domain validation on MNIST (Appendix H) supports the claim that the effect is a property of the GHN weight population rather than a robotics-specific artifact.
weaknesses: A critical missing baseline: the GHN itself is already width-agnostic and can generate weights for unseen architectures directly. The paper never reports how GHN-sampled policies perform on the unseen topologies relative to NNiT. Without this comparison, it is unclear whether the diffusion layer adds value over simply sampling the GHN, and the practical significance of the entire pipeline is left unresolved.

Circularity of the setup: NNiT learns to model a distribution that the authors themselves created with a GHN. The 'expert policies' are GHN-generated (not SGD-trained), top-100 filtered. The contribution is therefore a generative model over a synthetic, narrow distribution rather than over realistically trained networks; the pipeline demonstrably fails on SGD-trained weights (which lack alignment), so applicability to real model zoos is unestablished.

The headline claim of '>85% success on unseen architectures' rests on the top-10-of-100 selection protocol; the full-distribution means in Table 9 are 78.8%, 74.7%, and 54.9% (StackCubeEasy), so unconditional generation quality is materially weaker than the abstract implies.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair: SANE and D2NWG were designed for model zoos of SGD-trained networks and were retrained on GHN-generated data; SANE failing even on seen architectures (1–6% success) suggests an adaptation problem rather than a fundamental limitation of the approach, weakening the strength of the comparison.

The width-agnostic claim is narrow in practice: only MLPs, a vocabulary of three hidden widths {16, 32, 64}, four hidden layers, and a single fixed-depth family are evaluated; depth extrapolation and larger networks are asserted as future work. All 'unseen' topologies are width permutations within a very small combinatorial space (8 held-out configurations).

Evidence for structural alignment is largely qualitative (banding in heatmaps, Fig. 3/5); the one quantitative statistic (cross-seed correlation r ≈ 0.65) is reported only in the appendix and is modest, leaving the degree of alignment under-quantified.

Reproducibility concerns: no code or data release is mentioned, and the pipeline depends on many nontrivial components (128 GHNs, filtering thresholds, custom StackCubeEasy variant, MoNL adaptation) that would be hard to replicate from the text alone.

Some claims are speculative relative to the evidence, e.g., scaling to 'billion-parameter foundation models' and video-diffusion analogies in Section 7, which the experiments at MLP scale do not support.
